title: Arp 104 Keenan’s System (NGC 5216 & NGC 5218)
caption: Arp 104, Keenan's System, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
celestial: Arp 104, NGC 5216, NGC 5218 · constellation Ursa Major
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and H. Schweiker (WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Two spiral galaxies in the constellation Ursa Major are joined by a slender blue bridge. The pair is Arp 104, also called Keenan's System, with NGC 5216 at the bottom and NGC 5218 at the top.

The thin stream linking them is made of gas, and new stars are forming inside it. It was produced when the two galaxies swept past one another and their mutual gravity pulled gas out of them. The newborn stars in the stream are hot and massive, and their light is what gives it a blue color.

The stream stretches for about 150,000 light-years. Encounters like this one show that galaxies are not isolated islands. A close pass can reshape them, drag material across intergalactic space and set off fresh bursts of star formation far from either galaxy's center.
scale: The gas stream joining the two galaxies is about 150,000 light-years long, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter telescope observed Arp 104 through B, V and I filters, shown as blue, green and red respectively. B and V are visible light and I lies at the red edge of the visible, reaching into the near-infrared.
understand.eye: The faint gas stream is far too dim to see by eye. The camera's long exposures and the I filter, which extends toward light the eye barely senses, bring it out.
